notes: Behaves correctly but hardcodes reverse_proxy placeholder names into the generic caddyhttp CEL matcher via an exported UsesResponsePlaceholders(), a layering leak, and adds a redundant value-type switch case; it has good CEL-level tests but only a single integration case.

Behavior is correct, including the dynamic-name and prefix cases, but it hardcodes reverse_proxy placeholder names into the core caddyhttp CEL matcher (a layering leak) and adds a needless value-type switch case. Its doc edit also drops the is_transport_error mention.

Correct generic PlaceholderNames() API with a dynamic flag and classification in reverseproxy, and the doc comment update is relevant; the visitor stops collecting names once a dynamic call is seen, which leaves the names list incomplete (documented, so acceptable), and the tests are very thorough, including multi-case integration subtests.

Cleanly mirrors the reference with a generic PlaceholderNames API in caddyhttp and response classification in reverseproxy. It sensibly updates the RetryMatch doc and adds thorough table-driven unit and end-to-end tests covering every maintainer-specified case.

Closely mirrors the reference design, using ast.MatchDescendants/FunctionMatcher to collect ph() literal names and a dynamic flag, with classification kept in reverseproxy; tests cover both the CEL extraction and the retry classification, plus an integration test checking the upstream body (minor: Placeholders() returns the internal slice uncloned).

Matches the reference: it collects literal ph() names at provision time, flags non-literal names as dynamic, and classifies them with an exact-match list plus the header prefix in reverseproxy; minor nit is returning the internal slice uncloned, and tests are strong at both the unit and end-to-end level.

Records literal placeholder names plus a dynamic flag from the checked AST and exposes a clean generic ReferencesPlaceholder(predicate) API, with the response-placeholder list kept in reverseproxy; the classification table (escaped, prefix-lookalike, comprehension, dynamic concat, direct ph) and the end-to-end POST passthrough test are thorough.

An elegant ReferencesPlaceholder(predicate) API keeps the CEL matcher generic and handles dynamic names conservatively. The extensive classification table (including comprehensions and look-alike literals) plus the end-to-end regression test cover the spec well, though there is no celmatcher-level unit test.

Same caller-refresh approach as C2, placed inside the TaskID==0 branch; it emits whenever no jobs were updated, which is broader than needed but harmless; tests cover the nested handshake and both cancel and force-cancel emitting, but do not verify the waiter is released.

When a caller with children reaches cancelOneJob, this patch refreshes it from its children instead of hard-cancelling it, and it emits the run when only settling occurred; it fixes the root cause, but it always returns the caller as updated even when nothing changed, and it emits on every no-job-update cancel; the tests are thorough (nested handshake via UpdateTaskByState, plus cancel and force-cancel emit).

Any expanded caller is re-aggregated from its children rather than force-written cancelled, which is robust; it always returns the job even when unchanged and emits on every settle; tests are thorough and check attempt, run, stopped timestamps and checkRunConcurrency.

Same approach as C1 (refresh expanded callers in cancelOneJob), with an explicit `settled` flag driving the emit; it is correct but returns the caller unconditionally, and its tests are strong, including a real checkRunConcurrency check that the blocked waiter is re-emitted.

cancelOneJob now refreshes a caller instead of writing it cancelled when a direct child is still cancelling, which works for nesting because jobs are processed deepest-first; the run is emitted when settled with no job updates; tests cover the nested ack handshake and the concurrency waiter being released.

This patch only defers the caller when a direct child is still Cancelling; otherwise it falls back to the old stale-struct hard-cancel, which is narrower than the reference's reload-after-cascade but works; the tests cover the nested handshake and confirm that the concurrency waiter is woken.

Closest to the reference: cancelReusableCaller reloads and re-aggregates expanded callers and only reports real status changes, plus a correct emit for settled runs; the services test checks the emit but not that the waiting run is released.

Closest to the reference: callers in cancelReusableCaller are reloaded, refreshed only if not done, and reported only when their status actually changed, while unexpanded callers still go through cancelOneJob; the tests cover the nested handshake and force-cancel emit, but the latter only checks the mock and not the waiter.

Building the prefix config into AddCommonDiffArgs covers show, diff, stash show and the worktree diff in one place, which is DRY but a little implicit, and the parser changes mirror the reference; only command-arg test updates are visible.

Putting the prefix config inside AddCommonDiffArgs means every rendered diff (worktree, stash, show) is covered, and the explicit callers are updated too; the parser changes are correct. It also disables mnemonicPrefix, which the maintainer intended to leave alone, and the visible tests are mostly argument expectations.

The parser and its tests are solid, but WorktreeFileDiffCmdObj (the Files-panel diff from the issue) never gets the forced prefixes, so the new strip-first-component parser now resolves wrong or empty paths for diff.noprefix users.

Its config helper and parser match the reference closely, and the parser tests are thorough, but it never applies the helper to WorktreeFileDiffCmdObj. Users with diff.noprefix now get empty or wrong paths in the Files panel, the main staging flow.

The parser fix is correct: it strips any single-component prefix, reads rename/copy-to lines and splits the diff --git line on matching halves, and --src/--dst-prefix args force a/ b/ everywhere except `git stash show`, which still ignores a user's diff.noprefix.

Uses --src-prefix/--dst-prefix CLI options, which reliably override noprefix and mnemonic config, and adds strong parser tests plus an integration test. It skips stash show, so stash diffs still break path resolution under diff.noprefix.

It forces the prefixes through config on every diff lazygit reads or applies, including stash show and the SaveStagedChanges stash→apply pipe, and the parser generalization matches the reference; the parser tests are not visible in the truncated diff.

Covers every diff command lazygit runs, including worktree, stash show and the SaveStagedChanges pipe, and strips any single-component prefix in the parser. However, forcing diff.mnemonicPrefix=false overrides the user's display preference, which the maintainer wanted kept, and the visible tests are mostly command-arg updates.

Restores configured engine parameters instead of forcing a fresh discovery, which breaks the spec when an engine ID was supplied and fails a hidden test; it also adds struct fields, a redundant Close, and an unrelated mib_loader filesystem rewrite.

The core close-and-reconnect logic works for the default case, but on reconnect it restores the configured engine ID/boots/time instead of forcing fresh discovery, which deviates from the spec and likely explains the hidden test failure; it also adds struct fields that break unkeyed `GosnmpWrapper{...}` literals and ships an unrelated production rewrite of MIB path loading (mibDirFS).

The SNMP fix is correct and close to the reference, and it also resets ContextEngineID, but it bundles an unrelated production change to gosmi MIB path loading (os.DirFS) plus a package-wide TestMain, which is significant scope creep with its own regression risk.

The wrapper and Gather changes match the reference, and resetting ContextEngineID is a sensible addition, but the patch also swaps gosmi path registration for an `os.DirFS`-based filesystem plus a TestMain, a production change unrelated to the issue.

Closely matches the reference (immediate close on failure, Get/Walk reconnect, USM reset plus harmless key reset) with a clean helper and good tests across v1/v2/v3; the only scope creep is the TestSnmpInitGosmi path tweak, and the package suite failed for reasons that look environmental.

A clean implementation closely matching the reference, with harmless key resets, an immediate close on each failure and good wrapper/Gather tests; the only unrelated edit is a small tweak to TestSnmpInitGosmi, and the suite failure looks environmental (colon in temp path).

Correct fix that resets USM engine state, keys and ContextEngineID and reconnects in Get/Walk; however, the deferred close lets the remaining tables run on the stale connection for the rest of that gather, the unrelated TestSnmpInitGosmi edit adds scope, and the package suite failed (likely environmental, unconfirmed), while the tests are thorough and include a real UDP check of the discovery packet.

The wrapper fix is correct and also resets ContextEngineID and the keys, but it closes via a deferred flag only after all of the agent's tables, so recovery cannot happen within the same gather; tests are very thorough (they verify an actual discovery packet), with the same minor unrelated TestSnmpInitGosmi tweak as C3.

Correct and close to the reference (StatT.LinkTarget, lazy zip reads), but the squashfs root detection compares o.Remote() to a computed path and the zip Open has clunky EOF special-casing; the escape test's assertion is weak and the squashfs test needs mksquashfs.

Correct for both backends and passes all hidden tests, but the code is clunky: special EOF/offset handling in zip Open, and remote-comparison retries in squashfs New and NewObject; no handling of regular/symlink name collisions (same as the reference); strong tests including relative-target escape and squashfs copy.

Closest to the reference: lazy zip reads of member contents, squashfs links exposed with the suffix, List and NewObject agree, and regular .rclonelink files win over shadowing symlinks; the squashfs tests skip without mksquashfs and the docs addition is reasonable.

Implements --links handling for both zip and squashfs and keeps List and NewObject consistent; zip link targets are read lazily, as in the reference, and it adds sensible shadowing so a regular `X.rclonelink` member wins over symlink `X`; docs and thorough unit/archive-level tests (copy, escape, suffix collision) included.

Works and passes all hidden tests with thorough tests, but the root handling is convoluted: a zip root 'foo.rclonelink' can alias directory 'foo', roots without the suffix also resolve to symlinks, NewObject('dir.rclonelink') returns NotAFile, and link targets are read eagerly.

Clean in-memory link objects with proper range/seek handling, consistent NewObject lookup for squashfs, and good tests including a committed sqfs fixture and an escape test; however the zip root-suffix handling wrongly maps root `x.rclonelink` onto directory `x`'s contents, and link targets are read eagerly at mount time.

Adds a heavyweight case-insensitive LinkFilter in a new shared file that drops clashing symlinks, and even regular .rclonelink files, so hostile-archive symlinks are not listed (fails a hidden test). Squashfs NewObject now builds a full directory listing per lookup.

Over-engineered shared LinkFilter in a new archiver file, using case-insensitive clash rejection that drops symlinks and even regular `.rclonelink` files (contradicting the 'stays a regular file' requirement); squashfs NewObject now processes the whole directory on every lookup; fails a hidden test.

Careful implementation for both backends with consistent List/NewObject and good tests. However, it drops any symlink that clashes with another entry, so in the hostile-archive case the symlink is never listed, contradicting the spec and failing a hidden test; it also reads every link target eagerly at mount time.

Works for basic cases, but in zip it silently drops any symlink that has members 'inside' it or clashes with another entry instead of listing it like other backends, which deviates from the expected convention and fails a hidden test; it also pokes dirtree internals and eagerly reads link targets at mount time.

Working storage-lookup retention with correct chunk accounting and good restart/snapshot tests, but it uses optional variadic predicate hacks and includes unrelated go.mod/go.sum bumps and a go.work deletion.

It is functionally correct and has good tests. But it queries the exemplar storage RWMutex while holding the stripe and series locks, which can deadlock with ChunkSnapshot's iteration order. It uses variadic-parameter hacks and also carries the unrelated go.mod bump and go.work deletion.

The retention logic is clean: it collects protected label sets before taking any locks, adds a gcWithRetain wrapper, and counts chunks and mmap-ready state correctly, with excellent tests; however, it bumps go.mod/go.sum and deletes go.work, which is a serious unrelated change.

The fix works: it collects the label sets of exemplar-holding series before GC takes any locks, then retains and releases chunks in both GC paths, so it avoids lock-order problems and survives restarts. However, it bumps go.mod/go.sum and deletes go.work, which are unrelated and harmful changes, and it does not protect exemplars that are not yet committed.

The retention logic is plausible and it thoughtfully preserves WAL expiry for released samples, but it adds a method to the exported ExemplarStorage interface and changes the stripeSeries.gc signature, so hidden tests fail to run (0/3).

It adds a method to the exported ExemplarStorage interface and queries storage under the stripe and series locks without addressing deadlock. It also adds walExpiries tweaks that go beyond the fix. The non-variadic stripeSeries.gc signature change breaks the upstream tests, so the suite fails.

Looks up the in-memory exemplar store under the series lock to retain series on both GC paths and releases their chunks and appender correctly; the optional variadic predicate is a hack, and the ChunkSnapshot rewrite plus the global app-nil change in truncateChunksBefore are unneeded, since snapshot and truncation are already serialized by chunkSnapshotMtx.

It works by looking up the exemplar storage per series and thoughtfully reorders ChunkSnapshot to avoid the resulting lock-order deadlock. The cost is wider scope: a ChunkSnapshot rewrite and a global app=nil in truncateChunksBefore. The tests are decent, but the checkpoint helper is weak.
The retention logic is mostly right, but it iterates every stored exemplar on each GC, changes the gc signature (hidden tests 0/3), and includes unrelated go.mod/go.sum/go.work changes.

The retention logic is reasonable and avoids deadlock by pre-collecting labels. But it iterates every exemplar on each GC, makes non-variadic signature changes that break the upstream test compile, and includes the unrelated go.mod/go.work changes.

Closest to the reference: it tracks max exemplar ts on memSeries (on commit, replay and snapshot), skips that tracking on replay when exemplar storage is disabled, and releases chunks, appender and mmap-ready state correctly; it records only at commit rather than at append, and the new test is wedged under another test's doc comment.

This is the cleanest fix: a per-series max exemplar timestamp (using a flag bit) is recorded on commit, on WAL replay and on snapshot restore. Retention in gc and gcSeries releases chunks, the appender and the mmap-ready count, with no unrelated edits. Minor issues: protection is recorded at commit rather than append, and the new test hijacks another test's doc comment.

Per-series max-exemplar tracking close to the reference, but the ordinary-GC retention path does not clear series.app, so the removed chunk stays in memory; it also changes the gc signature, which breaks hidden tests (0/3, suite failed).

Tracking a per-series exemplar timestamp mirrors the reference. However, ordinary gc retains the series without clearing its appender, and protection is recorded only at commit. Changing the stripeSeries.gc signature breaks the upstream tests, so the whole suite fails.

A sound master-fd refcount redesign with registration-checked unlink, an abstract skip on both bind and close, and good tests, but restructuring the unixListener/unixSockets types makes it fail every hidden test and the package suite, and the rewrite is larger than needed.

A coherent master-fd refcount redesign that looks functionally correct on reading (last-holder unlink, guarded double close, race-safe under unixSocketsMu, abstract sockets skipped on both listen and close). It replaces the internal struct and map types, which broke every hidden test and the package suite, and it goes beyond the needed fix.

A minimal fix matching the reference: closes the leaked dup fd, unlinks the stored path under the lock, guards double close with ErrClosed and skips abstract names on close; however it lacks the GOOS check and the pre-bind abstract skip, so its own Linux abstract test (decoy file created before listen) would likely fail.

Closely mirrors the reference and passes the hidden tests: it closes the leaked dup'd fd, unlinks the real stored path under the lock, adds a CAS double-close guard returning net.ErrClosed, and skips '@' names on close. However, it does not stop the pre-listen unlink of '@' names, its '@' check is not limited to Linux, and its own Linux abstract-socket test would likely fail because listen unlinks the decoy file first.

The master-fd design with a separate state mutex and map-identity checks looks logically sound, but it also rewrites listenReusable, changes listenerPool registration for reused sockets, converts deleteListener to pointer semantics and edits listeners.go; this broad, risky refactor fails every hidden test and the package suite.

The logic looks sound and its tests are thorough. It is the most invasive rewrite: a second mutex, a restructured listenReusable, reused sockets now wrapped and counted in listenerPool (a behavior change), and an edit to listeners.go. That broad scope breaks all hidden tests and the package suite.

A clean shared-state refactor (master fd, refs under unixSocketsMu, GOOS-aware abstract check including the pre-bind unlink) that appears behaviorally correct and robust, but replacing the wrapper and map types breaks compatibility so all hidden tests and the package suite fail; it also changes deleteListener unnecessarily.

A similar master-fd redesign with a properly Linux-gated abstract check and good race and datagram tests. It also adds unrequested pointer-receiver and double-close changes to deleteListener/deletePacketConn. Its double Close returns a wrapped OpError rather than net.ErrClosed itself. The internal API changes fail all hidden tests and the package suite.
